source.citation: Federolf PA, Mills R, Nigg B (2008). Ice friction of flared ice hockey skate blades. Journal of Sports Sciences 26(11), 1201–1208. doi:10.1080/02640410802027360
source.notes: Abstract (PubMed 18608838), the primary for what it states (fidelity-gate §2.2): friction from the deceleration of an aluminium test sled on three test blades, initial speed 1.8 m/s, 53 kg on each blade; standard blades mu = 0.0071 (s = 0.0005). Secondary only, via Lever et al. 2022 p. 338, and so not entered as venue data: rocker 3.35 m, hollow 12.7 mm, indoor Olympic hockey rink, ice surface -5.7 to -4.9 C. Not stated in the abstract: whether air drag was subtracted. Expected is mu g, with g 9.81; u_m is the reported s times g. Stand-in for the sled: a 106 kg reference-height skater gliding flat on two feet, so each blade carries the sled's 53 kg; the model's glide friction does not depend on load, which Federolf found only slightly (ice-literature.md). The model's own air drag on that skater is inside the measured value, about 0.01 m/s^2 at 1.8 m/s by the open-constants arithmetic; the sled's drag is unknown. A hockey blade on a sled standing in for a figure skate: an L1 transfer. Checked after the first run, not used to choose anything: with the model's air drag removed the stand-in decelerates at 0.0589 m/s^2 (muGlide g), 15% under expected and still inside tolerance; with it, 0.0720. The verdict does not hang on the unknown drag handling.
